current_episode.title: From CAD to Smart Pumps: Glen Powell’s Journey in Engineering

guest.bio_context: Glenn Powell has been with Hydro for 13 years. He started his career during the global economic crisis in 2008-2009 with a master's degree, beginning as a CAD drafter and junior engineer at a manufacturing company before joining Hydro. He has worked in the reliability services group, pump test lab group, and currently works with the global engineering group on major projects and customer solutions.

Hey everybody and welcome to the Empowering Industry Podcast. I'm your host, Charlie Matthews-Karuth, and I'm excited to be here on the mic with my guest. anytime that I get to talk to a Hydro person, I'm really excited, especially one that's there in Chicago, because I love visiting. There's always something cool in that facility. And so I'll stop talking. Glenn, introduce yourself. Sure thing. Thanks for having me, Charlie. My name is Glenn Powell. I'm one of the senior engineers here at Hydro. And I've done a bunch of different things for the company and in the industry, worked in the reliability services group. I've worked with the pump test lab group, and currently I'm working with the global engineering group. So really taking on the big projects at Hydro and trying to help our customers in various different ways. Well, before you got to Hydro, what kind of got you into the industry? It was very interesting. When I first started my career, it was kind of during the global economic crisis in 2008 and 2009, I had a master's degree and nowhere to use it. So, you know, my first step into the industry was really doing CAD drafting work and working on assemblies for a manufacturing company. And one of the guys that I worked with there got a job with hydro, clued me in that it was a really nice company and wanted me to apply for a job here. And they took the chance on me, not being someone who's a pump expert from as far as my experience in the industry went. But they took a chance on me and I got a lot of great training and worked with a lot of great people here. And I've been with Hydro for 13 years now. So I went from lowly CAD drafter and junior engineer to learning a whole bunch of different skills in the industry. And now working with the global engineering team and connecting with a lot of different engineers that are in our group. Yeah, and that's so important. I've been there, like I said, to the facility several times. And the work that y'all are doing with the Centaur is global. It is locations all over. Can you tell a little bit about that program and how it works? Yeah, the Centaur has been a really exciting program for us. So we started this program from the perspective of a company that are pump repair focused, but with reliability experience and understanding how especially vibration data can be really important for diagnosing the health of machines and understanding how they're working. And so we partnered with a company who put us together with the technology to do wireless condition monitoring on pumps for our customers in the field, which allows us to take data on the vibrations that are happening on these pieces of equipment and keep an eye on them for the health of the machines. So really important set of data and sort of supplement a lot of the data that companies are already getting. People do a lot of route based monitoring where they'll take data on a maybe like a less critical piece of equipment once or twice a year. And if something is going wrong in between those times, they really have no idea. So the Centaur system allows us to put a sensor on those assets and get a stream of data that's much updated much more quickly. Usually once an hour could be once every five minutes. That's if it's absolutely necessary. But rather than having two points of data in a year, you get 24 points of data every day. And it allows us to understand what's going on with those pieces of equipment, keep our customers informed. And because of the technology has advanced a lot, it's available. You can look at all those pieces of data on your phone, on your laptop. If you're on a plane, you can access those data and alerts and understand something that's going on in the plant when you're halfway across the world. pending_qa.q: What is the Centaur system and how does wireless condition monitoring improve pump maintenance?
pending_qa.r: The Centaur is a wireless condition monitoring system that uses vibration data to diagnose machine health. Instead of traditional route-based monitoring with only two data points per year, the Centaur system puts sensors on assets to stream updated data every hour or every five minutes if necessary, providing 24 data points every day. This allows remote access via phone or laptop, and analysts at Hydro's development center in Chicago process the data to give customers actionable feedback for asset maintenance.

pending_qa.q: What testing capabilities does Hydro's pump test lab provide to the industry?
pending_qa.r: Hydro's test lab facility can accommodate up to 5,000 horsepower, up to 40,000 gallons per minute of discharge flow, and three to 4,000 PSI on the discharge. This fills a gap in the industry where large equipment manufacturers have test labs and small mom-and-pop shops have minimal testing capability. The test lab allows Hydro to connect engineering expertise with service capabilities to tackle challenging projects and prove out solutions for customers.

pending_qa.q: How is research and development being applied to smart pump technology for building systems?
pending_qa.r: Hydro has a current research and development project using the test lab to test smart capabilities of pumps for building circulations and heating and cooling cycles. The project puts smart pump algorithms to the test in a competitive shootout to determine what those technologies should really do and how to capture energy efficiency and savings. This represents an evolution from purely service-focused testing to innovation-driven research.

pending_qa.q: What is Hydro University and how does it address the skills gap in the pump and hydraulics industry?
pending_qa.r: Hydro University is a training initiative designed to transfer knowledge and skills to younger engineers entering the industry as older engineers retire. The program offers a mix of formats: live in-person training on-site with single or multiple companies, virtual meetings with customers, and pre-recorded training sessions such as basic vibrations courses that employees can access at their own pace. The goal is to ensure critical industry skills in hydraulics, mechanical systems, and reliability are not lost as the workforce transitions.

pending_qa.q: What ethical principle from Elemar McKay's engineering motto guides professional integrity in technical roles?
pending_qa.r: Glenn Powell learned from foundational Hydro engineer Elemar McKay that integrity and honesty are limited resources you only introduce once in your career. The principle is that if you do not know something, you say so and find out; misrepresenting knowledge erodes trust and integrity. In engineering, losing trust is especially dangerous because engineers design systems affecting people's lives, making perfect honesty essential compared to other professions.

pending_qa.q: What career advice should young engineers follow to advance beyond assigned tasks?
pending_qa.r: Young engineers should express curiosity and ambition beyond assigned work: show interest in being involved in projects, express willingness to help and learn, back up colleagues, and spend less time at desks and more time in shops and plants meeting people. Glenn Powell emphasizes that while newcomers have little knowledge, they can bring strong curiosity and ambition, and by connecting with people, going above and beyond, and being genuinely helpful without expecting reciprocal favors, they will advance significantly in their careers.
